analysis.one_liner: Lets insulin makers sell insulin straight to patients at current net prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its first committee referral and died when the 116th Congress ended, with no cosponsors and no vote ever scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directed the federal government to set up a way for insulin manufacturers to sell insulin directly to patients at the 'net price' — the lower price drugmakers actually receive after the discounts and rebates that middlemen currently negotiate. Today insulin's list price is often far higher than its net price, and patients who pay cash or have high deductibles can be billed the full list price at the pharmacy counter. The idea was to give manufacturers a legal channel to sell at their real price, cutting out the rebate system in between. It was one page long, never picked up a single cosponsor, and never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who pay cash for insulin or have high-deductible health plans, who can be charged the full inflated list price at the pharmacy even though the manufacturer's net price is much lower. Insulin makers would also gain a direct sales channel and a way to bypass pharmacy benefit managers and the rebate system.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require the federal government to create a mechanism through which insulin manufacturers may sell their products directly to consumers at current net prices [S2].

Net prices — what manufacturers actually collect after rebates and discounts — are typically much lower than the list prices insulin makers advertise, so a direct-at-net-price channel could lower what cash-paying and high-deductible patients pay at the counter.

analysis.who_pays: The bill did not force prices down and did not include new funding or mandates; the main losers if it had passed would have been the middlemen in the insulin supply chain — pharmacy benefit managers, insurers, wholesalers, and pharmacies — who collect margin on the gap between list and net prices. Insulin manufacturers would have kept their current net revenue.

drawbacks.text: The bill only permitted sales at 'current net prices' — it did not lower prices, cap them, or require manufacturers to actually use the mechanism, so it would have worked only if drugmakers volunteered to sell direct.

Selling directly to consumers would still leave patients responsible for navigating coverage, and patients with insurance that has favorable insulin cost-sharing might have done no better, or worse, than under their plan.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the insulin patients who today pay the full list price, this was a low-cost idea with real potential: it mandated nothing and spent nothing, it simply created a door drugmakers could walk through to sell at their true price. But it was also a very thin bill — one sentence long — that depended entirely on insulin manufacturers choosing to participate, and it would have left the underlying rebate system untouched. As a solution to insulin prices it was modest; as a signal of willingness to act, it was what its legislative record showed: no cosponsors joined and no committee took it up.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, and neither ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jeff Fortenberry (R-NE) introduced the bill on December 10, 2019, near the end of the first session of the 116th Congress [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and the next day to that committee's Subcommittee on Health [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and it attracted zero cosponsors [S4] [S5].
The bill expired on January 3, 2021, when the 116th Congress ended, without ever leaving committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died quietly with no opposition ever on the record, the parties better off are the status quo: insulin manufacturers keep the list-price system that lets uninsured and high-deductible patients be billed full price, and pharmacy benefit managers and insurers keep the rebate intermediation the bill would have let drugmakers route around. Insulin patients got nothing either way.

for.name: Rep. Jeff Fortenberry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 10, 2019; no colleague joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 10, 2019, sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no one besides the Republican sponsor signed on, so no partisan pattern for or against the bill appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill gave drugmakers a legal channel to sell directly to patients at the net price they already receive, which would have helped the patients who get billed full list price. But participation was voluntary and prices were not reduced, so manufacturers stood to gain a new market without giving up their pricing system.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers
industries.note: A direct-to-consumer sales channel at net prices would let insulin bypass the rebate negotiations these intermediaries run, and the gap between list and net prices is where much of their leverage and margin sits. The bill died before any of them had to take a position on the record.

The bill's subject list includes retail and wholesale trades because direct manufacturer-to-consumer sales would route around the wholesalers and pharmacies that currently mark up and dispense insulin. Cash-pay patients would have been the winners if manufacturers had used the channel.
